newsitem.title: GERMANY: German IBIS DAX ends thin trade almost unchanged.
newsitem.headline: German IBIS DAX ends thin trade almost unchanged.

text.p: A more stable day on the currency markets helped calm the German share market on Tuesday and the blue chip IBIS DAX index recouped early losses to end the day little changed.
The IBIS DAX ended electronic trade up 2.55 points, or 0.07 percent, at 3,671.16 points.
Earlier, the 30-share DAX closed bourse trade down 2.42 points at 3,665.01 points, having dipped as low as low as 3,648.45 early in the session.

Worries about monetary union and the future of Bonn's ruling coalition, still in the grips of a damaging dispute about how to plug Germany's gaping deficit hole, unsettled the market from the start and kept turnover minimal.
"The dollar came to the rescue," said a Frankfurt trader.
"But the environment is not the best at the moment. People won't buy into an uncertain market," he added.
The dollar steadied after a period of fluctuation against the mark, trading around 1.71 marks through the day.

Dollar volatility always unsettles the German share market, since so many top German corporates -- notably carmakers, engineering and chemical firms -- depend on the U.S. export market for large amounts of their sales.

Dollar-sensitive car shares such as Volkswagen and BMW both stabilised initially after Monday's losses. VW maintained gains to end the day up 6.90 marks at 1,195 marks, but BMW was hit by profit-taking later on and ended electronic trade down 14 marks at 1,373.
On a day of thin trading, telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom stood out as relatively healthy as traders noted it had passed a technical resistance level at 40.50 marks.
Telekom share ended the day up 1.10 marks at 41.40 marks.
But traders said the outlook was uncertain with much likely to depend on how other markets finally interpret the worrying signals from France on monetary union.

On Monday, the new French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said he wanted to delay an agreement on the stability pact designed to ensure budgetary discipline under monetary union, triggering worries the project will be delayed.
